title: Becoming physical at twelve: defending his violin in new neighborhoods
summary: He describes fending off bullies who wanted his violin or bicycle in semi-integrated neighborhoods, and how his father taught him to avoid fights.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Shed some light on that mystery. Well, tell me. You said that there were other interests. What about athletics at that age?

Well, I -- for some reason or other that's why I play so much importance on age 12 in my life. It's because this was when I started everything. Athletics and everything. All of a sudden I became a man, you might say, at the age of 12, because I was able to decide for myself getting back to the fisticuffs. All right, my father had taught me so many things, mental things and spiritual things, and now at the age 12 I became aware of myself as a physical man, and where I had to also protect myself, which is a very important thing when you move around from city to city, from environment to environment, where you are predominantly more or less in the what you call now the ghetto era -- area, you know.

Of course I might embellish on this too, because my father for some reason or other was always able to have some sort of relationship where during the course of my childhood we lived in semi-integrated neighborhoods. Now, this is way back in those days, you know. We've got to be talking
You know. And I remember -- many times we lived in what you call a semi-integrated area, where I associated with many white people. And this was unusual then, you know.

But however, naturally, we were more or less predominantly in black neighborhoods, but they were always nice neighborhoods and of course my father and mother being cultured people, our home was as clean and nice as the next person's, you know. But it was this time that I became aware of my athletic ability because there were times I had to protect myself as a boy. You know, when you carry a violin under your arm, and you're not too big -- you know, I was not a great specimen of Charles Atlas type, you know, and fact of the matter is I was always sorry that I didn't weigh about 100 pounds more, you know. I think I could have even made a little more noise in the new neighborhoods.

But many times when I'd come down the street with my violin, many of the boys would challenge me, you know, I mean want to take my violin away from me. Well, now everything they would say to me would be, I could take. They'd call me names or whatever or not, but when they grabbed that violin boy, they were in trouble.
You -- I guess you just felt so strongly about it that you were able to assert yourself.

Listen, when they put their hands on that violin, that was it. I put the violin down and picked up a brick. But this was very -- I didn't have any -- I remember -- I didn't have what you call violent incidents, but there were -- you know, as little boys are, I was very fortunate, I think, by the training of my father, of what to say and how to walk away from fights when necessary and when possible. The combination of those things, I think, made it -- so I don't remember ever having any real violent fights or anything like that. But I remember several incidents where I had to assert myself, and it paid off.

I had a bicycle during this time, my father had bought me wagons, and all the things that boys should have, skates and things. And I'd have these scuffles in new neighborhoods, you know, they'd come in there and they'd think you're a minister's son and you're a little bit on the weak side, and they'd try to take your bicycle. In fact I had some larger boys who did take my bicycle once and my father had to go get it for me. This is a -- understandable, particularly in the days where you could be a man and walk down the street and some kids will take your bicycle now.
